'''Alma Levant Hayden''' (March 30, 1927 – August 2, 1967) was an American [[chemist]], and one of the first [[African Americans|African-American]] women to gain a [[scientist]] position at a science agency in [[Washington, D.C.]]<ref name="Rossiter 1982" /> She joined the [[National Institutes of Health]] (NIH) in the 1950s.<ref name="Rossiter 1982" /><ref name="NIH History">{{cite news|author=Office of NIH History|title=Hidden Figures in Paper Chromotography|work=The NIH Catalyst|publisher=National Institutes of Health|url=https://irp.nih.gov/catalyst/25/2/from-the-annals-of-nih-history|access-date=May 7, 2017}}</ref> Hayden graduated from [[Howard University]] with a [[master's degree]] in chemistry, and became an expert in [[spectrophotometry]].<ref name="NIH History" /> She published work on infrared and other techniques for analyzing chemicals in a range of journals. Hayden was appointed Chief of the Spectrophotometer Research Branch in the Division of Pharmaceutical Chemistry at the [[U.S. Food and Drug Administration]] (FDA) in 1963, and may have been the first African-American scientist at the FDA.<ref name="Rossiter 1982" /> Hayden came to national attention in 1963 when she led the team that exposed the common substance in [[Krebiozen]], a long-controversial alternative and expensive drug promoted as anti-cancer.<ref name="LA Times 1963" />

==Education==
Alma Levant was born in [[Greenville, South Carolina]], on March 30, 1927<ref>{{Cite book |last=Cattell |first=James Mckeen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pDU7AAAAMAAJ&q=%22+Hayden,+Alma+%22+Carolina |title=American Men of Science: A Biographical Directory |publisher=Bowker |year=1966}}</ref> and graduated with honors in 1947 from [[South Carolina State College]], a historically black college in [[Orangeburg, South Carolina]].<ref name="Pittsburgh Courier 1947">{{cite news|title=S.C. acclaims Honors students|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/40023852/|access-date=May 7, 2017|work=The Pittsburgh Courier|date=May 17, 1947|page=11}}</ref> Originally planning to be a nurse, she found herself so interested in chemistry that she "just didn't want to part from it".<ref name="Howard Success Panel">{{cite book|author=Women's Bureau|author2=U.S. Department of Labor|author3=National Association of Colored Women's Clubs|last4=Howard University|title=Report of the World of Work Conference on Career and Job Opportunities, eld at Howard University, Washington, D.C., July 26–28, 1962|date=1963|publisher=U.S. Dept. of Labor, Women's Bureau|location=Washington, DC|page=12|chapter-url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/011422640|access-date=May 7, 2017|chapter=Success story panel}}</ref> She gained a master's degree in chemistry from [[Howard University]].<ref name="NIH History"/>

==Career==
Hayden joined the National Institute of Arthritis and Metabolic Diseases at the NIH.<ref name="NIH History" /> The above photograph was taken there in 1952, showing her working with a technique called paper [[chromatography]], spraying [[reagent]] on liquids dropped onto paper to detect precursors to [[steroids]].<ref name="NIH History" /><ref name="NIH Record">{{cite news|title=Detecting cortisone precursors|url=https://nihrecord.nih.gov/PDF_Archive/1952%20pdfs/19520407.pdf|access-date=May 7, 2017|work=The NIH Record|issue=IV No 7|publisher=National Institutes of Health|date=April 7, 1952|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181010011026/https://nihrecord.nih.gov/PDF_Archive/1952%20pdfs/19520407.pdf|archive-date=October 10, 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Hayden steroids 1956" />

In the mid-1950s Hayden moved to the FDA, where she may have been the first person of color to work at the Agency.<ref name="Rossiter 1982">{{cite book|last1=Rossiter|first1=Margaret W.|title=Women scientists in America|date=1982|publisher=Johns Hopkins University Press|location=Baltimore|isbn=9780801857119|page=283|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=i7xDqk0_HTQC}}</ref> There had reportedly been a reluctance to employ African-Americans there because scientific officers may have to give testimony in courts, and there was concern about how this would be received in some parts of the U.S. In 1963, Hayden became Chief of the Spectrophotometer Research Branch in the Division of Pharmaceutical Chemistry.<ref name="Rossiter 1982" />

In 1962 in the wake of the [[Thalidomide tragedy]], the [[Kefauver Harris Amendment]] increased the FDA's role in ensuring drug safety.<ref name="Peltzman, Sam 1051">Peltzman, Sam. [https://www.jstor.org/stable/1830639  An Evaluation of Consumer Protection Legislation: The 1962 Drug Amendments]. The Journal of Political Economy, Vol. 81, No. 5. (Sep. – Oct. 1973), pp. 1051.</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.fda.gov/AboutFDA/WhatWeDo/History/CentennialofFDA/CentennialEditionofFDAConsumer/ucm093787.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090709193833/http://www.fda.gov/AboutFDA/WhatWeDo/History/CentennialofFDA/CentennialEditionofFDAConsumer/ucm093787.htm |url-status=dead |archive-date=July 9, 2009 |title=Promoting Safe and Effective Drugs for 100 Years |work=The Kefauver-Harris Drug Amendments |publisher=U.S. Food and Drug Administration }}</ref> With these provisions in place, the FDA sought to identify the ingredients in [[Krebiozen]], a controversial and expensive alternative cancer treatment.<ref name="Time" /><ref name="St Louis Dispatch 1963">{{cite news|last1=Loory|first1=Stuart H.|title=Student found clue to Krebiozen identity shortly after starting work on 20,000 spectrographs|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/142117312/|access-date=May 7, 2017|work=St. Louis Post-Dispatch|date=September 8, 1963|page=24}}</ref> Hayden assigned students in her branch the task of seeing whether spectrometer images of Krebiozen matched any of the 20,000 alphabetically-listed images on file at the FDA. On September 3, 1963,<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|last=Kelly|first=John|date=August 2017|title=A cure-all for cancer? Early federal chemist proved them wrong.|url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/307618431|newspaper=The Washington Post|id={{ProQuest|307618431}}}}</ref> a likely match was quickly found in the "C"s: a common substance, [[creatine]].<ref name="LA Times 1963">{{cite news|title=Criminal prosecution prepared for anti-cancer drug inventor|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/164053567/|access-date=May 7, 2017|work=Los Angeles Times|agency=via New York Herald Tribune|date=September 8, 1963}}</ref><ref name="St Louis Dispatch 1963" /> It occurs in the body at a far higher level than contained in Krebiozen, and had been shown to have no impact on cancer in animals.<ref name="LA Times 1963" /><ref name="St Louis Dispatch 1963" />

Spectrophotometry and [[crystallography]] studies were conducted independently by three teams, including scientists from [[MIT]].<ref name="Press & Sun-Bulletin 1963">{{cite news|last1=McGaffin|first1=William|title=U.S. government convinced judgment on drug is correct|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/254206502/|access-date=May 7, 2017|work=Press and Sun-Bulletin (New York)|date=September 11, 1963}}</ref> The discovery was announced at a press conference.<ref name="St Louis Dispatch 1963" /><ref name="History FDA">{{cite book|title=History of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration|date=June 17, 1980|publisher=U.S. FDA|location=Silver Spring, Maryland|url=https://www.fda.gov/downloads/AboutFDA/WhatWeDo/History/OralHistories/SelectedOralHistoryTranscripts/UCM262793.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130802195544/http://www.fda.gov/downloads/AboutFDA/WhatWeDo/History/OralHistories/SelectedOralHistoryTranscripts/UCM262793.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 2, 2013|access-date=May 7, 2017}}</ref> Hayden's report is detailed in the [[Congressional Record|U.S. Congressional Record]].<ref name="Senate record">{{cite book|title=Congressional Record – Senate|date=December 6, 1963|publisher=U.S. Congress – Senate|location=Washington, DC|page=46|url=https://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/pkg/GPO-CRECB-1963-pt18/pdf/GPO-CRECB-1963-pt18-3-1.pdf|access-date=May 7, 2017}}</ref> Hayden testified at the lengthy criminal trial of the promoters of Krebiozen,<ref name="Time">{{cite magazine|magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |url=http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,842474,00.html |title=The Krebiozen Verdict |date=November 2, 1966 |access-date=May 7, 2017 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080222005152/http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0%2C9171%2C842474%2C00.html |archive-date=February 22, 2008 }}</ref><ref name="Daily Times 1965">{{cite news|title=Says Krebiozen is worthless|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/86081562/|access-date=May 7, 2017|work=The Daily Times (Ohio)|date=September 2, 1965}}</ref> Stevan Durovic and [[Andrew Conway Ivy|Andrew C. Ivy]].<ref name=":0" />

==Personal life==
Hayden married a fellow NIH research chemist, Alonzo R. Hayden.<ref name="NIH History" /> Alonzo Hayden was from West Virginia, with a PhD from the [[University of Wisconsin]].<ref name="Alonzo Hayden obituary">{{cite news|date=March 24, 1993|title=Alonzo R. Hayden, research chemist|newspaper=Washington Post|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1993/03/24/obituaries/1bca24ae-7cad-4c30-aa64-5eea0b7f5591/|access-date=May 7, 2017}}</ref> He had also undertaken postgraduate studies at Howard University, and worked at the NIH from 1952 to 1958.<ref name="Alonzo Hayden obituary" /> Alonzo also worked in the [[US Department of Agriculture]] for the research facility in Beltsville, MD.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news|last=Weil|first=Martin|date=March 1993|title=Obituaries; Polykarp Kusch Dies; Won Nobel in Physics|url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/307618431|newspaper=The Washington Post|id={{ProQuest|307618431}}}}</ref>

The Haydens had two children, Michael and Andrea.<ref name="Alonzo Hayden obituary" /> Alma Hayden died of cancer on August 2, 1967.<ref name="books.google.com">{{cite web|year=1967|title=Journal of the Association of Official Analytical Chemists|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qmkXAQAAIAAJ&q=Alma+Levant+Hayden+1967}}</ref><ref name="WaPo">{{cite news|last1=Kelly|first1=John|date=August 26, 2017|title=The doctor said it could cure cancer. The federal chemist proved that it couldn't.|newspaper=Washington Post|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/the-doctor-said-it-could-cure-cancer-the-federal-chemist-proved-that-it-couldnt/2017/08/26/62e72986-88d0-11e7-a94f-3139abce39f5_story.html|access-date=27 February 2020}}</ref> She loved doing science throughout her life.
